text.text: Your practice in one place. Start with Inquiries to reply to today, then Sessions for the day's schedule and unfinished notes, and Statements for payments. Operational tracking only; clinical notes and records stay in your clinical record system.
Reaching out for therapy is hard. A warm, prompt reply within one business day makes the difference between someone starting care and giving up.
Add the inquiry with a first name or initials, what they are looking for (individual, couples, family, teen, assessment), how they plan to pay and where they found you. Set
Reply by the method they used. If they called, call back; if they wrote, write back and offer a short phone consultation.
Ask what is bringing them in now, in a sentence or two. Do not start therapy on the phone.
Ask about safety: "Are you having thoughts of harming yourself or anyone else?" If yes, follow your crisis protocol and give the crisis line number before anything else.
Check fit: the clinician's specialty, availability, location or telehealth, and fees.
Explain fees plainly. For self-pay clients, explain that they will receive a good faith estimate of expected costs before the first session.
Intake booked with a clinician who fits
Intake paperwork sent: consent, privacy notice, fee policy, cancellation policy, release forms if needed
Good faith estimate sent to self-pay and sliding-scale clients
When you are not the right fit
Say so kindly and give two or three specific referrals.
and write which referrals you gave.
If no clinician has space, offer the waitlist with an honest estimate of the wait. Check the waitlist every week; people who wait longer than a month should get a call with referrals.
Speak with the parent or guardian first; check who holds the right to consent in your state, and that both parents' consent is in place when required.
"Thank you for reaching out, Winnifred. I have openings on Tuesday mornings and Thursday evenings. Would you like a 15-minute call tomorrow to see whether we are a good fit?"
The intake sets the frame for the work: consent, expectations, fees and the first treatment plan. A clean intake prevents most later billing and boundary problems.
Fee, cancellation and no-show policy signed
Good faith estimate sent (self-pay and sliding scale);
Insurance verified if billing insurance: mental health benefits, copay, deductible, whether prior authorization is needed, telehealth coverage
Releases of information signed if the client wants you to speak with another provider
Telehealth link and a backup phone number if the session is online
Review confidentiality and its limits in plain words.
Screen for safety and document the plan if risk is present.
Agree initial goals and how often to meet.
Book the next four sessions at a steady weekly time.
Treatment plan written and signed by the client where required
date set (every 90 days is common, sooner if a payer requires it)
Client status moved from Intake to
Agree the policy on secrets between partners before the first individual contact.
Decide who the statement goes to and who pays.

Jasper's intake is today at 2 pm by telehealth. His consent came back two days ago; his insurance needs no prior authorization. After the session, Emeka signs the note, writes the plan and sets the first review for 90 days.
Late notes are the most common reason a practice cannot bill, and they become an ethical and legal risk if records are requested. A simple daily habit fixes it.
Every session's note is drafted the same day and signed within 48 hours. Insurers may ask to see notes; a claim without a signed note should not go out.

text.text: Daily (10 minutes at the end of each clinical day)
Filter Sessions to completed today with Note status not Signed.
Draft each note before leaving. Set it to
Review and sign yesterday's drafts. Set them to
Front office lists every completed session from the week whose note is not signed and sends each clinician their list.
Notes older than seven days are discussed in supervision or the practice meeting.
What a good progress note covers
Date, service code, length and whether it was telehealth.
What was worked on, linked to a treatment plan goal.
The client's response and any change in risk.
The plan for the next session.
Keep it brief and factual. Write it as if the client may read it one day, because they may.
Their notes need the supervisor's co-signature. Add the supervisor review to the weekly list and do not bill until both signatures are in.
When a session is a no-show or late cancel
Write a short administrative note anyway: the time, the attempts to contact the client and the outcome. It protects the client and the practice.
Rhea sees six clients on Mondays. At 5:30 she drafts all six notes, then signs Friday's two drafts before leaving. Her Note status column shows nothing older than one day.
Talking about money is part of good care. Clear estimates up front and steady monthly statements mean fewer awkward conversations later.
Good faith estimates for self-pay clients
Before the first session, send a written estimate of expected costs: fee per session, expected number of sessions for the first months, and any assessment fees.
If the plan changes a lot (for example, adding couples sessions), send an updated estimate.
On the first business day of the month, create a statement for each client with sessions last month. Include each date, service code and fee, and late cancel fees under your policy.
Insurance clients who pay out of network receive a superbill they can submit themselves.
and set the due date (15 or 30 days).

The administrative side of a therapy practice: people reaching out, intakes, the week's sessions, notes that still need signing, and statements. Clinical notes themselves stay in your secure records system; nothing here should hold what was said in session.
